blocks.heading: Footpath-erosion investigation
blocks.text:
A footpath investigation can test whether path width or exposed depth varies with visitor use. Define the measured feature: width between stated path edges differs from the depth of an incision below a reference line. Use a tape across the path at a consistent orientation, and a level reference and ruler where depth is measured. Obtain permission and avoid unsafe slopes or obstructing users.

![Footpath stations, width and depth measurement, and record sheet](../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-2.3-038-PROC-answer.png)

blocks.text: A common investigation tests whether footpath erosion decreases with distance from a tourist hot spot such as a car park, viewpoint or lodge. Most visitors walk the first stretch of path, so trampling is concentrated there. Use systematic sampling: place measurement stations at regular intervals, for example every 20 m, along the path away from the hot spot. Regular spacing covers the whole path evenly and avoids choosing only the worst-eroded places; random sampling might leave gaps, while stratified sampling suits paths with distinct sections, such as steep and flat stretches.

At each station, measure width between the edges of bare ground with a tape held at right angles to the path. For depth, lay a ranging pole across the path and measure down to the surface with a ruler at five equally spaced points, then take the mean. Record slope, surface material and drainage, because steep or wet sections can erode faster.

Plot distance on the horizontal axis and mean width or depth on the vertical axis. Describe the trend, then suggest a reason for any anomaly, such as a steep or waterlogged section. Pedestrian counts at each station over the same period test whether use also falls with distance, although a short count shows present use, not the years of use that formed the path.

For example, mean widths of 240, 180, 130, 150 and 90 cm at 0, 20, 40, 60 and 80 m show a general decrease away from the hot spot, with an anomaly at 60 m to explain. Width and depth can show different patterns, so judge each measured feature separately.
